prompt:
You probably learned in school that our solar system has nine planets, and Pluto is the last one. Then in 2006, Pluto lost its planet status and became a dwarf planet. Many of us assumed there was nothing big left in this story. But on October 27, 2026, news arrived that reopened it. Beyond Pluto’s average distance, about 46 astronomical units away, a new dwarf planet candidate has been found, named 2026 ED138. And the most shocking part is that it was already out there, nobody had just seen it. So the question is, how did something this big stay hidden until now?

Paragraph 2

The answer lies with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which sits on Cerro Pachon in Chile. On the evening of October 13, scientist Matthew Holman was running a search code that matches billions of moving detections against each other. The code flagged something so bright and so far away that Holman could hardly believe it. His first move was to check whether he or the code had made a mistake. Then the team dug through the data and found 20 more observations, so the object was seen 30 times across 20 nights, from March 4 to July 11, 2026. Even more, older images traced its path back to 2016, giving more than 10 years of orbit. The reason is that it sat near a part of the Milky Way with millions of stars, and it got lost among them.

Paragraph 3

Now let’s see how big it is. Rubin’s team estimates ED138 could be between 600 and 1,500 kilometers across. For comparison, Pluto’s diameter is about 2,377 kilometers. So ED138 is smaller than Pluto, but it could be anywhere from a quarter to two thirds of its size. In distance, it is beyond Pluto’s average: ED138 is currently about 46 astronomical units out, while Pluto’s average is about 40. One astronomical unit is the distance from Earth to the Sun. At that distance, sunlight takes a little over 6 hours to reach it. Its orbit is tilted about 25 degrees from the plane of the solar system, which suggests Neptune’s gravity may have pushed it out of place at some point. But remember, it is still just a candidate, not confirmed. Infrared observations are needed to settle it.

Paragraph 4

If ED138 is confirmed, it will be the sixth dwarf planet, joining Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake. A new name in a very small family. And Rubin has only just begun: its big survey started in June 2026, and the telescope will scan the entire southern sky again and again for 10 years. According to Holman, there could be more hiding in places older surveys left behind. Think about it, our own solar system may still hold worlds nobody has even seen. We kicked Pluto out of the planet club, and the universe answered by dropping another hidden sibling right in front of us. What do you think, should ED138 get dwarf planet status? Let us know in the comments.

parts.title: The Nine Planet Myth
parts.brief: Viewers see nostalgic retro classroom footage showing solar system charts ending with Pluto. The narrative establishes how generations were taught that Pluto marked the absolute outer edge of our cosmic neighborhood. This sets up the initial historical context before introducing modern astronomical surprises.

parts.title: Pluto's Demotion
parts.brief: Archival footage and news headlines from 2006 highlight Pluto's controversial reclassification into a dwarf planet. Building on the previous context of textbook solar system models, this part shows how humanity assumed the story of major outer bodies was largely complete.

parts.title: The October Announcement
parts.brief: Sleek modern motion graphics display breaking news alerts from October 27, 2026, revealing a major astronomical update. Expanding on the idea of a settled solar system, this segment introduces the sudden arrival of unexpected deep-space data.

parts.title: Meet 2026 ED138
parts.brief: A dramatic 3D render zooms past Pluto to 46 astronomical units away, revealing a new dwarf planet candidate named 2026 ED138. Connecting directly to the breaking news alert, the visual illustrates the sheer distance and physical characteristics of this newly recognized world.

parts.title: Hiding in Plain Sight
parts.brief: The video presents the central puzzle using scale comparisons of 2026 ED138 against well-known solar system bodies. Following the physical reveal of the dwarf planet, this part highlights the mystery of how such a substantial object evaded detection for decades.

parts.title: The Eyes of Cerro Pachón
parts.brief: Cinematic drone footage reveals the high-altitude Vera C. Rubin Observatory atop Cerro Pachón under the clear Chilean night sky. Transitioning from the mystery of the hidden object, this section introduces the facility designed to solve it.

parts.title: Why Past Telescopes Failed
parts.brief: Animated visual comparisons contrast narrow traditional telescope field-of-views with wide-sky observations. Building on the introduction of the Rubin Observatory, this part explains how 2026 ED138's faint light and slow orbital crawl allowed it to slip past legacy instruments.

parts.title: The Wide-Sky Revolution
parts.brief: Viewers see visualizations of Rubin's massive digital camera rapidly scanning panoramic swathes of space to track tiny moving highlights. Continuing the explanation of optical advancement, this segment demonstrates how continuous mapping flagged the elusive object.

parts.title: Redefining the Kuiper Belt
parts.brief: An updated dynamic solar system model populates with 2026 ED138 alongside neighboring trans-Neptunian objects. Evolving from the mechanics of discovery, this part explores what the candidate tells us about the true density and secrets of the outer system.

parts.title: The Unfinished Map
parts.brief: The camera pulls back to show a vast cosmic horizon filled with uncharted territory, leaving viewers with an inspiring message about ongoing discovery. Summarizing the shift from 2006 to 2026, the finale reinforces that our celestial neighborhood is still full of surprises.
